Anatomical white matter tracts span the cortical hierarchy to support cognitive diversity

The superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) is a massive association fiber bundle running anterior–posterior parallel to the cortical sheet, linking frontal cortex with parietal, occipital, and temporal association areas. It exemplifies the long-range corticocortical wiring that allows distributed cortical models to exchange information without routing through subcortical hubs.

Relationship with ventral stream?

A stream refers to a major, relatively segregated pathway through which information flows across different regions of the brain, typically from primary sensory areas toward higher-order association areas. Each stream is usually defined by its anatomical connections, the kind of information it processes, and its functional roles in perception, cognition, or action. Streams are not just highways for information-they are partially parallel, often recurrent, and interact with one another and with other brain systems. Modern research increasingly views them as dynamic, flexible networks that route and transform information according to current goals and contexts, rather than as rigid, linear processing lines.

The classic examples are the dorsal ("where/how") and ventral ("what") visual streams, but similar stream-based architectures have been identified in auditory, somatosensory, and even language domains. In these systems, streams can be thought of as distinct but interacting circuits that handle complementary aspects of sensory input. For instance, in vision, the ventral stream processes object identity, while the dorsal stream processes spatial location and guides movements. The auditory system, likewise, splits into a ventral stream for recognizing sounds and a dorsal stream for mapping sounds to actions or locations.

Two visual processing streams

The primate visual cortex routes information through two major, partially overlapping highways that spring from primary visual cortex (V1). The ventral stream arcs along the inferior temporal lobe (V1 -> V2 -> V4 -> inferior temporal cortex) and builds increasingly invariant, high-dimensional representations of "what" is in view-objects, faces, textures, written words, scene categories, and their semantic associations. The dorsal stream rises dorsally through the parietal lobe (V1 -> V2 -> MT/MST -> posterior parietal cortex) and emphasizes "where" and "how": motion, depth, spatial layout, eye and limb position, and the real-time transformations needed to guide actions such as grasping or saccades. Classic neuropsychology, single-cell recordings, and neuroimaging established this functional dichotomy in the 1980s-1990s and it remains a central organizing principle of vision science today 2.

Over the last decade, the picture has shifted from two neat, serial hierarchies to a pair of densely interconnected, recurrent heterarchies embedded in widespread cortical and subcortical networks. The dorsal and ventral streams are not rigid pipelines that progressively refine information in a fixed order; instead, they consist of regions whose responses are shaped by context, goals, and cross-stream interactions. Many areas once thought to belong exclusively to one stream are now known to communicate extensively with the other, and both are directly influenced by inputs from memory systems, motor structures, and prefrontal areas. Rather than building a single unified percept, each region contributes a partial, task-relevant interpretation that may be used independently or in coordination with others depending on behavioral demands. 2.

Two somatosensory streams

Somatosensory processing is done through at least two largely parallel ascending streams: a medial "lemniscal" channel that relays fine-grained proprioceptive and cutaneous position signals through dorsal column nuclei (in the spine) and VPL thalamus to S1 and on into parietal areas supporting sensorimotor control; and a more lateral/paralemniscal channel that carries multimodal object and affective touch information toward S2, insula and temporal operculum for haptic object recognition and affective valuation. Dense axonal reconstructions show distinct projection motifs all the way to cortex, supporting genuine stream-like segregation 3.

Somatosensory Dorsal Stream

Starting in primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and coursing through posterior parietal cortex (especially intraparietal areas) to premotor cortex, this stream represents the body’s configuration and object location. It encodes spatial and postural information (proprioception and tactile cues) in an egocentric reference frame, and projects this to motor planning areas. Functionally, it forms a "body-in-space" map used to guide actions (e.g. reaching, grasping) and sensorimotor coordination 4

Somatosensory Ventral Stream

From S1 through secondary somatosensory cortex (S2) and insula into medial temporal areas (including hippocampus), this pathway encodes the intrinsic properties of touched objects. It builds invariant representations of object shape, texture and identity through touch. Anatomically, it connects to limbic/hippocampal regions (via S2 and insula) to support haptic object memory and recognition. In effect it underlies tactile "what" processing, forming memory traces of objects felt (akin to (and interacting with) visual ventral stream but via touch) 4.

Two auditory streams

The auditory cortex is now widely accepted to host a "what/where-how" split that mirrors the visual dorsal-ventral dichotomy. A ventral route courses from primary A1 through the middle and anterior superior temporal gyrus into anterior temporal pole and inferior frontal areas; it builds increasingly invariant spectro-temporal templates for identifying voices, phonemes, words and environmental sounds, essentially mapping acoustic patterns onto meaning. In parallel, a dorsal pathway arcs posteriorly into the parietal operculum and premotor cortex, where sensory traces are mapped onto articulatory or spatial motor codes-essential for vocal imitation, phonological working memory and sound-source localisation; it supports sensorimotor integration in speech and music: learning to produce sounds, guiding vocal tract movements, and real-time feedback control of articulation. Lesion patterns such as conduction aphasia and modern tractography of the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculi clinch the dissociation between the dorsal and ventral streams.

Two language streams

The dual stream model of language processing follows the same fundamental architectural principle as the general auditory system - a ventral "what" stream for recognition/comprehension and a dorsal "how" stream for sensorimotor transformation; language piggy-backs on exactly the same scaffold but adds a layer of linguistically specific computations, especially combinatorial semantic processing in the ventral stream.

The core insight-traced all the way back to Wernicke- is that the auditory word representation in posterior superior temporal gyrus (STG) simultaneously feeds two diverging routes: an auditory-to-conceptual (A -> C) branch for comprehension and an auditory-to-motor (A -> M) branch for production/monitoring. Hickok & Poeppel formalised these as the ventral and dorsal language streams.

Ventral Stream (Comprehension)

After bilateral spectro-temporal analysis in primary auditory cortex, activity flows along mid/posterior STG and the upper STS where phonological features are extracted. From there it fans antero-ventrally into posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG)-a "lexical interface" that maps sound patterns onto distributed semantic memory-and further into the anterior temporal lobe, which supports combinatorial conceptual processing. The network is almost bilateral, with only a mild ( 60/40) leftward bias. Functionally it answers the questions what word is that? what does it mean? In your auditory map this is the linguistic specialisation of the ventral "what" stream.

Dorsal Stream (sensorimotor integration & production)

Phonological representations in STG/STS project posteriorly to a Sylvian-parietal-temporal hub called area Spt in the planum temporale; Spt transforms auditory codes into articulatory ones and stays active both when you listen and when you silently rehearse speech or hum a melody. From Spt the signal ascends the supramarginal gyrus to premotor cortex and into the inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis, BA 44) and dorsal M1, completing a loop that compares predicted and heard speech to fine-tune articulation. This stream is strongly left-lateralised ( 90% of right-handers), mirroring your auditory "how" tract but specialised for the rapid, learned articulatory gestures of language.

Two attention and executive streams

The dorsal attention network (intraparietal sulcus <-> frontal eye fields) is bilaterally organized and implements sustained, goal-directed orienting and sets gain on modality-specific cortices, while the ventral attention network (temporo-parietal junction <-> ventral frontal cortex) is strongly right-lateralized acts as an interrupt/reset circuit that re-orients the system to unexpected but behaviorally relevant stimuli. Contemporary fMRI/MEG work shows dynamic coupling between the two nets rather than a simple hierarchy, underscoring their stream-like but interactive nature. 5.

At the level of prefrontal cortex itself, a dorsal-ventral axis of functional specialization mirrors these attention streams. Petrides and colleagues have shown that mid‐dorsolateral PFC (areas 46 and 9/46) underlies higher‐order monitoring and manipulation of information-holding abstract representations "on line" and comparing them against goals-whereas mid‐ventrolateral PFC (areas 45 and 47/12) mediates first‐order executive processes such as the active selection, comparison, and judgment of mnemonic and perceptual inputs 6. Anatomically, this aligns with the finding that the dorsal visual stream (spatial/action information) projects preferentially to dorsolateral PFC, while the ventral visual stream (object/feature information) projects to ventrolateral PFC 7. Thus, PFC itself is not a homogeneous executive control center but rather comprises parallel "streams" tuned either for abstract, spatially organized monitoring (dorsal) or for the selection and comparison of concrete stimulus features (ventral).

Two episodic memory streams

Episodic memory research has converged on two cortico-hippocampal "medial temporal lobe streams"-the anterior-temporal (AT) and posterior-medial (PM) systems-that feed the hippocampal formation from opposite ends. The AT stream (perirhinal -> anterior temporal pole / ventrolateral PFC) emphasizes item identity, emotion and social semantics; the PM stream (parahippocampal / retrosplenial -> precuneus / vmPFC) conveys contextual frameworks (space, situation, self). Effective-connectivity analyses during naturalistic recall show the two systems exert separable influences on the subjective vividness and content of memory, vindicating Ranganath & Ritchey’s dual-stream proposal. 8, 9

Multiple value/reward streams

The macroscopic picture starts with four largely parallel dopaminergic projection systems. The nigrostriatal tract (substantia nigra -> dorsal striatum) biases vigor and habit formation; the mesolimbic tract (VTA -> ventral striatum, amygdala) encodes incentive motivation and appetitive learning; the mesocortical tract (VTA -> prefrontal and cingulate cortices) carries a slower, state-value and cognitive-control signal; and the tuberoinfundibular tract modulates hypothalamic endocrine set-points. Anatomically these bundles share a midbrain origin yet remain largely non-overlapping up to their cortical or striatal termini, and functional imaging or fiber-photometry confirms that each stream carries a distinct "flavor" of reward information. 10

Zooming in, even the mesolimbic axis fractures into finer sub-streams. Medial VTA cells projecting to nucleus accumbens shell emit textbook reward-prediction-error bursts, whereas lateral VTA neurons projecting to accumbens core or dorsolateral striatum fire more transient salience or movement-gain signals and can be optogenetically separated in both rodents and primates. Single-cell sequencing and connectomics now map these populations onto discrete molecular lineages, arguing that the "dopamine RPE" is only one branch of a broader, parallel value architecture 11, 12.

Opponent valence rides its own tracks. The lateral habenula-rostromedial tegmental ("anti-reward") stream suppresses VTA firing when outcomes are worse than expected, while medial habenula and specific hypothalamic-VTA pathways convey positive or homeostatic value. Recent stress-induction studies show that hyperactivity of the negative-valence stream can globally re-weight cortical processing within minutes, underscoring its independence from the classical reward pathways 13, 14

Downstream, cortico-basal-ganglia loops are themselves arranged in parallel limbic, associative and sensorimotor circuits that feed into ventral, dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum, respectively. Each loop implements a distinct cost-benefit calculus-motivation, goal-directed planning, or habitual efficiency-yet they all reconnect to cortex through thalamus, giving the organism multiple, simultaneously running value estimators that can be blended or weighted according to context 15, 16.

Other neuromodulators furnish additional streams: serotonergic raphe projections encode punishment expectancy and temporal discounting; noradrenergic locus-coeruleus fibers broadcast surprise and arousal; endogenous-opioid hotspots in nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex register consummatory "liking". These systems interdigitate with, but do not collapse into, the dopaminergic tracks, reinforcing the idea that the brain maintains multiple, parallel value channels tuned to different statistics of the environment and body.
